docs.title: lilota
docs.text:
lilota is a lightweight Python library for executing long-running tasks in the background without the overhead of full-fledged task queue systems. While those tools are powerful and valuable, lilota focuses on scenarios where a simpler approach is sufficient.

It is designed for simple, asynchronous task execution with minimal setup and overhead.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Run long-running tasks
  • Simple API and minimal configuration and setup
  • Persistent task state stored in a database
  • No message broker required
  • Suitable for applications that use background jobs, i.e. web applications.

docs.title: When to use lilota
docs.text:
Use lilota when your application needs to run tasks that take time, such as:

  • image or file processing
  • report generation
  • sending emails
  • heavy computations

Instead of blocking the request, lilota lets you start the task in the background.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install lilota

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
This example demonstrates how to add two numbers using a function that runs in the background.

This could, of course, also be a function that generates a report or performs a heavy computation. For simplicity, we will just add two numbers.

First, we have to create a script that has an instance of a worker (LilotaWorker). This worker registers one or several task-functions that can be executed later by a scheduler.

docs.title: myscript.py
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from lilota.worker import LilotaWorker


@dataclass
class AddInput():
    a: int
    b: int


@dataclass
class AddOutput():
  sum: int


worker = LilotaWorker()


@worker.task
def add(input: AddInput) -> AddOutput:
  return AddOutput(input.a + input.b)


def main():
  worker.start()


if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()

docs.title: Integration of lilota
docs.text:
The script created above is passed to a Lilota instance for execution.

Note: The script must start the worker by calling worker.start(). Each worker process runs the script as its entry point, and a script that ends without starting a worker is treated as a fatal error (see lilota.error).

That instance can start multiple processes, each of which executes the script once. By default, it starts one worker process. You can specify the number of workers for a Lilota instance with number_of_workers. A worker executes one task at a time, so this is the number of tasks that can be executed in parallel. See Number of workers for what a worker costs.

In this example, we use two model classes: one for input arguments and one for the output. These models should typically be defined in their own module and shared between Lilota and LilotaWorker.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from lilota.core import Lilota
from lilota.models import Task
import time


@dataclass
class AddInput():
    a: int
    b: int


@dataclass
class AddOutput():
  sum: int


lilota = Lilota(
  script_path="sample/myscript.py",
  number_of_workers=8
)


def main():
  # Start lilota
  lilota.start()

  # Schedule a task
  task_id = lilota.schedule("add", AddInput(a=2, b=3))

  # Wait one second because Lilota runs in the background and decides when to pick up a task.
  # This is normally not needed. We do it here because we want to wait until the task 
  # has been executed.
  time.sleep(1)

  # Retrieve task information from the database and print the result
  task: Task = lilota.get_task_by_id(task_id)
  print(f"We add the numbers 2 and 3: ")
  print(task.output)


if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
lilota executes tasks in a managed way. All information processed by lilota are stored in various database tables in order to make it transparent to the user what is happening in the system.

If you do not specify a connection string in the db_url then lilota uses sqlite:///lilota.db and stores the data in a SQLite database. lilota uses SQLAlchemy and therefore all databases that are supported by SQLAlchemy can be used here.

docs.title: Creating the tables
docs.text:
You do not have to create the tables yourself. Every scheduler and worker brings the database up to date when it is created, using lilota's own Alembic migrations. To do it without starting anything, for example in a deployment step:

from lilota.db.alembic import upgrade_db

upgrade_db("postgresql+psycopg://user:password@localhost:5432/myapp")

Several processes can do this at the same moment, for example the worker processes of a web server that each create a Lilota, or several containers that start together. Only one of them creates the tables. The others notice that they came too late, wait a second and then find the database up to date.

For the same reason an error in a migration is not reported at once: lilota tries 5 times, with a second in between, before it gives up with Could not update the database.

docs.title: Sharing a database with your application
docs.text:
lilota can live in the same database as your application, even if your application manages its schema with Alembic too.

All tables lilota creates start with lilota_. lilota records its migration revision in its own table, lilota_alembic_version, rather than in Alembic's default alembic_version. Your application keeps alembic_version for itself, and neither one reads or changes the other's revision.

One thing has to be set up in your application. Alembic's autogenerate compares the database with your models. It sees the lilota_ tables, does not find them in your models and generates a migration that drops them. Tell autogenerate to ignore them in your application's migrations/env.py:

def include_object(object, name, type_, reflected, compare_to):
    return not (type_ == "table" and name.startswith("lilota_"))

# ... and in both context.configure(...) calls:
context.configure(
    ...,
    include_object=include_object,
)

lilota_alembic_version starts with lilota_ as well, so this filter covers it too.

docs.title: Upgrading from lilota 1.1.1 or older
docs.text: Up to 1.1.1, lilota recorded its revision in alembic_version. Nothing has to be done by hand: on the first start after the upgrade, lilota moves its revision from alembic_version to lilota_alembic_version. It drops alembic_version if nothing else is left in it. Revisions that are not lilota's are left where they are, so a revision of your application's in the same table is untouched.

docs.title: Cleaning up
docs.text:
lilota deletes nothing by itself. Every task, every retry, every log entry and every node stays in the database, and the row of a task keeps its input, output and error.

To delete what is old, call cleanup from time to time, for example once a day:

from datetime import timedelta

deleted = lilota.cleanup(older_than=timedelta(days=30))
print(deleted)  # {'tasks': 1250, 'log_entries': 310, 'nodes': 12}

cleanup deletes the rows that are older than the given age:

Table Deleted The age is counted from lilota_task tasks with the status completed, failed, expired or cancelled the time the task ended or expired lilota_log all entries the time the entry was written lilota_node nodes with the status dead the time the node was last seen

It never deletes

  • a task that is waiting or being executed
  • a failed or expired task that still waits for its retry
  • a node that is alive

cleanup works in every mode, and lilota does not have to be started for it.

Two things to know:

  • A node that has ended gets the status dead when a worker that is running notices that it is gone. Until then it is not deleted.
  • A retry keeps the ID of the task it retries in previous_task_id. That task can be deleted before the retry is.

docs.title: Node (lilota_node)
docs.text:
This table stores information about the scheduler responsible for scheduling tasks in the system, as well as the workers responsible for executing them.

Column Description id Unique identifier of the node (UUID). name Optional human-readable name of the node. type Type of node (scheduler or worker). status Current lifecycle status of the node (e.g., starting, running, stopped, dead). created_at Timestamp when the node record was created. last_seen_at Timestamp of the most recent heartbeat received from the node. Used to detect stale or dead nodes.

docs.title: NodeLeader (lilota_node_leader)
docs.text:
This table stores information about the worker that currently acts as the leader.

Column Description id Primary key for the leader record (typically a single-row table). node_id Identifier of the node currently acting as the cluster leader. lease_expires_at Timestamp indicating when the leader lease expires if not renewed.

docs.title: Task (lilota_task)
docs.text:
This table stores information about the tasks executed by the system.

Column Description id Unique identifier of the task (UUID). name Name of the registered task function to execute. pid Process identifier associated with the task execution. status Current status of the task (created, scheduled, running, completed, failed, expired, cancelled). run_at Timestamp indicating when the task becomes eligible for execution. attempts Which attempt this task is: 1 for a task that was scheduled, 2 for its first retry, and so on. max_attempts How often the task is executed at most. The first execution counts. retried_at Timestamp when a retry was created for this task. Empty if the task was not retried. previous_task_id For a retry: identifier of the task it retries. Empty for a task that was scheduled. timeout Maximum execution duration allowed for the task before it should be considered timed out. expires_at Optional timestamp (UTC) after which the task is considered expired and should no longer be executed. progress_percentage Current progress of the task expressed as a percentage (0–100). start_date_time Timestamp when the task started execution. end_date_time Timestamp when the task finished execution (successfully or with failure). input JSON payload containing the input parameters for the task. output JSON payload containing the result produced by the task. error JSON object describing an error if the task execution failed. locked_by Identifier of the worker node currently holding the execution lock for the task. locked_at Timestamp when the task was locked by a worker for execution.

docs.title: LogEntry (lilota_log)
docs.text:
lilota supports logging and stores all log messages in this table.

Column Description id Unique identifier of the log entry. created_at Timestamp when the log message was created. level Logging level (e.g., DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR). logger Name of the logger that produced the message. message Log message text. process Identifier of the process that produced the log entry. thread Identifier of the thread that produced the log entry. node_id Optional reference to the node associated with the log entry. task_id Optional reference to the task associated with the log entry.

docs.title: Migration version (lilota_alembic_version)
docs.text:
This table is managed by Alembic and stores which lilota migration the database is at. See Sharing a database with your application for why it is not called alembic_version.

Column Description version_num Revision of the latest applied lilota migration.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
In Lilota, external code is executed. Errors that occur in the executed scripts are normally caught and handled by the worker.

If an error cannot be caught by the worker, or if an exception stops parts of Lilota and leaves the system in an inconsistent state, this is reflected in the error property of the Lilota class. This property returns the last fatal error encountered by the system that was not handled by a worker.

If a worker process fails, the error is the last lines the process has written to stderr, which usually is the traceback of the exception. The same lines are shown in the output of your application. See Worker output.

The Lilota class also provides two methods to:

Check whether a fatal error has occurred (has_failed) Wait until a fatal error occurs (wait_for_failure), which blocks execution

docs.title: After a fatal error
docs.text: A fatal error stops all workers. No task is executed anymore until the workers are started again.

docs.title: Being told about a fatal error
docs.text:
Your application does not have to ask has_failed again and again. Pass a function as on_fatal_error, and lilota calls it when a fatal error has happened:

def on_fatal_error(error: str):
  print(f"lilota has stopped all workers: {error}")


lilota = Lilota(
  script_path="myscript.py",
  on_fatal_error=on_fatal_error
)

The function gets the error that the error property returns. It is called in a thread of lilota, so it should return quickly, and it must not call stop.

docs.title: Scheduling a task
docs.text:
schedule still stores a task after a fatal error, so that the task is not lost. It is executed as soon as workers are running again. Because that can take long, schedule writes a warning to the lilota_log table:

The task 'add' (0d3c...) was scheduled, but no worker can execute it: a fatal error has stopped all workers. Call start() to start them again

docs.title: Starting the workers again
docs.text:
When the cause of the error is gone, call start. You do not have to call stop first:

lilota.start()

start starts the workers again and resets the fatal error: has_failed returns False and error returns None, until the next fatal error.

docs.title: A task raises an exception
docs.text:
This is an error the worker handles. It is not a fatal error.

The worker stores the exception in the error column of the task and sets the status of the task to failed. Then it goes on with the next task. If the task has attempts left, it is retried. See Retry mechanism.

docs.title: A worker is killed
docs.text:
A worker process that is killed is replaced by a new one. This is not a fatal error either. It happens when

  • a task runs longer than its timeout. The worker stops itself, because that is the only way to end the task. See Task timeout.
  • the process is terminated by a signal, for example by the operating system because it used too much memory.

What happens to the task the worker was executing depends on why the worker was killed:

  • The task ran longer than its timeout: it gets the status expired and is retried if it has attempts left. See Retry mechanism.
  • The process was terminated by a signal: the task is given back and executed again by another worker, about 20 seconds later. See Worker maintenance.

docs.title: A worker keeps dying
docs.text:
A worker that stopped itself because a task ran longer than its timeout is replaced at once.

A worker process that died for another reason is replaced after a waiting time of 1 second. If the new process dies as well, the waiting time doubles every time: 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds.

If the process dies again after the fifth restart in a row, another restart would not help. Lilota stops all workers and reports a fatal error:

The worker script 'myscript.py' was restarted 5 times in a row, and its process died every time. The last time it was killed by the signal SIGKILL.

If the process has written something to stderr, these lines follow.

A worker that has been running for a minute before it died is not one that keeps dying. For the process that replaces it, the counting and the waiting time start again.

docs.title: The database cannot be reached
docs.text:
lilota keeps everything in the database. If the database cannot be reached for a while, for example because it is restarted, the workers keep running. This is not a fatal error, and nothing has to be restarted.

  • A worker waits and tries again until the database is back. It tries as often as it looks for new tasks when there are none, which is every 5 seconds by default (max_task_heartbeat_interval).
  • A task that is being executed is not interrupted. If it ends while the database cannot be reached, its result is stored as soon as the database is back.
  • The heartbeats of the nodes fail in that time and go on afterwards.

A log entry cannot be written to the database in that time either. It is written to stderr instead, as one line:

lilota: ERROR: The database cannot be reached. The worker waits and tries again (the log entry could not be written to the database)

Methods that you call, like schedule and get_task_by_id, raise the error of the database to your application.

Note: A worker that is started while the database cannot be reached fails, for example the worker that replaces a worker that was killed. That is a fatal error, as described in the next section.

docs.title: Worker script fails
docs.text: If the worker script itself ends with an error, for example because of an exception while it is imported, starting it again would fail the same way. Lilota stops all workers and reports a fatal error. The error is what the process has written to stderr.

docs.title: Worker script does not start a worker
docs.text:
Each worker process runs the script passed as script_path as its entry point. The script has to start the worker itself:

def main():
  worker.start()


if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()

A started worker runs until it is stopped by Lilota. If the script ends without calling worker.start(), Lilota stops all workers and reports a fatal error:

The worker script 'myscript.py' exited without starting a worker. Did you forget to call worker.start()?

docs.title: Upgrading from lilota 1.2.1 or older
docs.text:
Up to 1.2.1 a worker process that died was replaced within a second, however often that happened. A worker that died every time it was started was restarted once a second for as long as the application was running, and no error was reported.

Nothing has to be changed in your application. Be aware that a worker that was killed is now replaced after 1 to 2 seconds, and that a worker that keeps dying ends in a fatal error after about half a minute.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
lilota aims to be simple. To understand what this means in practice, it helps to briefly look at the main classes involved.

Lilota is built around three concepts: 1. Schedule tasks 2. Run workers 3. Store state in a database

Most applications only need a single Lilota instance to handle all three.

docs.title: Lilota (lilota.core)
docs.text:
Lilota is the main entry point for applications using Lilota. It allows tasks to be scheduled and workers to be started to execute those tasks.

Internally, it creates a LilotaScheduler instance and a worker manager responsible for starting worker processes. Each process runs a script that creates an instance of LilotaWorker.

Most applications only need the Lilota class. The scheduler and worker classes are described below for advanced deployment scenarios.

Create a lilota instance:

lilota = Lilota(
  script_path="sample/myscript.py"
)

Here, myscript.py is the worker script. The worker script registers the task functions that workers are allowed to execute.

The script is executed by worker processes managed by a worker manager. When a Lilota instance is created, the worker manager is automatically configured and can be started with lilota.start().

An example of such a script can be found here.

Start lilota:

lilota.start()

This starts the scheduler and the worker manager.

Schedule a task:

task_id = lilota.schedule("add", AddInput(a=2, b=3))

The schedule function creates a task entry in the database and returns the ID of the stored task. The task is not executed at once: a worker that is free picks it up within 5 seconds. A worker that finds no task waits longer every time before it looks again, up to max_task_heartbeat_interval. To shorten that, pass a smaller max_task_heartbeat_interval to the LilotaWorker in your worker script.

Retrieve task information including the output (if available):

task: Task = lilota.get_task_by_id(task_id)
add_output = AddOutput(**task.output)
print(add_output.sum)

docs.title: LilotaScheduler (lilota.scheduler)
docs.text:
In some applications, it is useful to separate task scheduling from worker management. Worker processes can then be managed by a separate application.

Create a scheduler:

from lilota.core import Lilota

scheduler: LilotaScheduler = Lilota.scheduler()

docs.title: Workers
docs.text:
If you need a separate application to manage worker processes, you can create a worker manager directly:

from lilota.core import Lilota

worker_manager = Lilota.workers(
  script_path=str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "workerscript.py")
)

docs.text: A full example using the class methods can be found here: 7-using-factory-methods

docs.title: LilotaWorker (lilota.worker)
docs.text:
LilotaWorker implements the worker responsible for retrieving scheduled tasks and executing them.

Multiple workers can run simultaneously. Each worker independently polls the database for available tasks. When a worker retrieves a task, it locks the task, preventing other workers from executing it. This ensures that each task is executed exactly once.

Workers can run:

  • on the same machine
  • inside containers
  • on different machines in a distributed system

docs.title: Number of workers
docs.text:
A Lilota instance starts one worker process, unless you tell it to start more:

lilota = Lilota(
  script_path="sample/myscript.py",
  number_of_workers=4
)

A worker executes one task at a time. number_of_workers is therefore the number of tasks that can be executed in parallel. With one worker, a task that takes ten minutes lets every other task wait for ten minutes.

Every worker is a Python process of its own, so more workers are not free:

  • Memory: about 60 MB for a worker that waits for tasks, plus everything your worker script imports.
  • Database connections: about 2 for every worker, plus 1 for the scheduler.
  • Database load: every worker writes a heartbeat every 5 seconds, and looks for the next task at least every 5 seconds.

The workers are started by the process that creates the Lilota instance. A web server that runs several processes of your application starts them once for each of these processes. 4 application processes with number_of_workers=4 are 16 worker processes and about 36 database connections. PostgreSQL allows 100 connections by default.

The number of workers cannot be greater than the number of CPU cores * 5.

docs.title: Upgrading from lilota 1.2.1 or older
docs.text:
Up to 1.2.1 a Lilota instance without number_of_workers started as many workers as the machine has CPU cores. That number was different on every machine, and in a container with a CPU limit it was still the number of cores of the host.

Now it starts one worker. If your application does not set number_of_workers and executes several tasks in parallel, set the number you need. Otherwise the tasks are executed one after the other.

docs.title: Communication between nodes
docs.text:
All nodes communicate through the shared database. If you do not specify a connection string, lilota will use sqlite:///lilota.db by default. This creates a SQLite database.

For production-ready applications, we recommend using a more advanced database that handles multiple processes efficiently. We recommend PostgreSQL. However, since lilota uses SQLAlchemy to access the database, any database supported by SQLAlchemy can be used.

For many applications this setup is sufficient. However, some scenarios require horizontal scaling. In these cases, multiple Lilota instances can run across several servers. They still connect to the same database.

docs.title: Clocks on several machines
docs.text:
Every node uses the clock of its own machine: when it stores the time it was last seen, when it sets the time at which a task expires, and when it compares such a time with the current time. Nodes on one machine share one clock. If your nodes run on several machines, the clocks of these machines have to be in sync, for example with NTP.

A difference of less than a second does not matter. A larger one does:

  • The timeout of a task is set with the clock of the worker that executes it and checked with the clock of the leader. If the clock of the leader is ahead, a task is expired and retried before its timeout is over, while it is still being executed.
  • A worker that is alive is taken for dead when its clock is behind the clock of the leader by about the node timeout, which is 20 seconds by default. Its tasks are given back and executed a second time. See Worker maintenance.

docs.title: Lilota
docs.text:
High-level interface for Lilota task scheduling and worker management.

The Lilota class coordinates a scheduler instance and a pool of worker processes that execute user-defined task scripts.

A scheduler manages task persistence, distribution, and node heartbeats, while worker processes execute tasks defined inside the provided script.

Workers are started as separate Python processes that run the provided script file as a module entry point.

Source code in lilota/core.py 
class Lilota:
    """High-level interface for Lilota task scheduling and worker management.

    The Lilota class coordinates a scheduler instance and a pool of worker
    processes that execute user-defined task scripts.

    A scheduler manages task persistence, distribution, and node heartbeats,
    while worker processes execute tasks defined inside the provided script.

    Workers are started as separate Python processes that run the provided
    script file as a module entry point.
    """

    @classmethod
    def scheduler(cls, db_url: str = DEFAULT_DB_URL, **kwargs) -> LilotaScheduler:
        """Create a LilotaScheduler instance.

        Args:
          db_url (str): Database connection URL.
          **kwargs: Additional keyword arguments passed to the constructor.

        Returns:
          LilotaScheduler: Configured LilotaScheduler instance.
        """
        lilota = cls(
            mode=LilotaMode.SCHEDULER,
            db_url=db_url,
            script_path=None,
            number_of_workers=0,
            **kwargs,
        )
        return lilota._scheduler

    @classmethod
    def workers(
        cls,
        script_path: str,
        number_of_workers: int = 1,
        db_url: str = DEFAULT_DB_URL,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        """Create a Lilota instance running only worker processes.

        Args:
          db_url (str): Database connection URL.
          script_path (str): Path to the worker script.
          number_of_workers (int): Number of worker processes to spawn.
            Defaults to 1.
          **kwargs: Additional keyword arguments passed to the constructor.

        Returns:
          Lilota: Configured instance in worker-only mode.
        """
        return cls(
            mode=LilotaMode.WORKERS,
            db_url=db_url,
            script_path=script_path,
            number_of_workers=number_of_workers,
            **kwargs,
        )

    def __init__(
        self,
        db_url: str = DEFAULT_DB_URL,
        *,
        mode: LilotaMode = LilotaMode.ALL,
        script_path: str = None,
        number_of_workers: int = 1,
        scheduler_heartbeat_interval: float = 5,
        scheduler_timeout_sec: int = 20,
        process_manager_interval: float = 1.0,
        stop_worker_timeout: int = 60,
        logging_level=logging.INFO,
        on_fatal_error: Callable[[str], None] = None,
    ):
        """Create a new Lilota runtime instance.

        Args:
          db_url (str):
            Database connection URL used by the scheduler.

          mode (LilotaMode, optional):
            Execution mode controlling whether the scheduler, workers,
            or both are started. Defaults to ALL.

          script_path (str):
            Path to a Python script that defines and registers Lilota tasks.
            Each worker process executes this script as its entry point.
            The script must call ``worker.start()``. If it ends without
            starting a worker, all workers are stopped and the failure is
            reported through ``error``.

          number_of_workers (int, optional):
            Number of worker processes to spawn. A worker executes one task
            at a time, so this is the number of tasks that can be executed
            in parallel. Defaults to 1 and cannot exceed the number of CPU
            cores * 5.

          scheduler_heartbeat_interval (float, optional):
            Interval in seconds between scheduler node heartbeats.
            Defaults to 5 seconds.

          scheduler_timeout_sec (int, optional):
            Time in seconds after which a node is considered inactive
            if no heartbeat is received. Defaults to 20 seconds.

          stop_worker_timeout (int, optional):
            Maximum time in seconds to wait for worker processes to
            exit gracefully before they are forcefully killed.
            Defaults to 60 seconds.

          logging_level (int, optional):
            Logging level used by the scheduler. Defaults to logging.INFO.

          on_fatal_error (Callable[[str], None], optional):
            Function that is called when a fatal error has stopped all
            workers. It gets the error, which is also what ``error``
            returns. It is called in the thread that monitors the workers,
            so it should return quickly, and it must not call ``stop()``.
        """
        if mode in (LilotaMode.WORKERS, LilotaMode.ALL):
            if number_of_workers <= 0:
                raise ValueError("number_of_workers must be > 0 in WORKER or ALL mode")

            number_of_cpus = cpu_count()
            max_workers = number_of_cpus * 5
            if number_of_workers > max_workers:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"number_of_workers cannot be greater than {max_workers}"
                )

        self._db_url = db_url
        self._mode = mode
        self._script_path = script_path
        self._number_of_workers = number_of_workers
        self._process_manager_interval = process_manager_interval
        self._stop_worker_timeout = stop_worker_timeout
        self._process_manager_heartbeat: Heartbeat = None
        self._process_manager = ProcessManager(on_fatal_error=self._handle_fatal_error)
        self._on_fatal_error = on_fatal_error
        self._error = None
        self._error_event = threading.Event()
        atexit.register(self._process_manager.stop_all)

        if mode in (LilotaMode.SCHEDULER, LilotaMode.ALL):
            self._scheduler = LilotaScheduler(
                db_url=db_url,
                node_heartbeat_interval=scheduler_heartbeat_interval,
                node_timeout_sec=scheduler_timeout_sec,
                logging_level=logging_level,
            )

        self._node_store = NodeStore(self._db_url, None)
        self._task_store = TaskStore(self._db_url, None)
        self._log_store = LogStore(self._db_url)
        self._is_started = False

    @property
    def error(self):
        """Return the last fatal error encountered by the system.

        The error is reset when ``start()`` starts the workers again.

        Returns:
          Any: The error object or message captured from a worker process,
          or None if no error has occurred.
        """
        return self._error

    def has_failed(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether a fatal error has occurred.

        Returns:
          bool: True if a fatal error has been detected, otherwise False.
        """
        return self._error_event.is_set()

    def wait_for_failure(self, timeout=None):
        """Block until a fatal error occurs or a timeout is reached.

        Args:
          timeout (float | None, optional): Maximum time in seconds to wait.
            If None, waits indefinitely.

        Returns:
          bool: True if a failure occurred before the timeout, False otherwise.
        """
        return self._error_event.wait(timeout)

    def _handle_fatal_error(self, error):
        self._error = error
        self._error_event.set()

        if self._on_fatal_error:
            try:
                self._on_fatal_error(error)
            except Exception:
                # The function belongs to the application. An error in it must not
                # end the thread that monitors the workers.
                traceback.print_exc()

    def _reset_error(self):
        self._error = None
        self._error_event.clear()

    def start(self):
        """Start the configured Lilota components.

        Depending on the selected mode, this method:
          - Starts the scheduler (SCHEDULER, ALL)
          - Spawns worker processes (WORKER, ALL)
          - Starts process monitoring for workers (WORKER, ALL)

        After startup, the instance is ready to schedule and/or execute tasks.

        After a fatal error the method starts the workers again. ``stop()`` does
        not have to be called first. The fatal error is reset: ``has_failed()``
        returns False and ``error`` returns None, until the next fatal error.
        """
        if self._is_started:
            # A fatal error has stopped the workers. Everything else is still running.
            if self.has_failed():
                self._reset_error()
                self._start_workers()
            return

        self._reset_error()

        if self._mode in (LilotaMode.SCHEDULER, LilotaMode.ALL):
            self._start_scheduler()

        if self._mode in (LilotaMode.WORKERS, LilotaMode.ALL):
            if not self._script_path:
                raise ValueError("script_path must be provided in WORKER or ALL mode")
            self._start_workers()
            self._start_process_manager()

        self._is_started = True

    def _start_scheduler(self):
        self._scheduler.start()

    def _start_workers(self):
        # Start scripts
        for _ in range(self._number_of_workers):
            self._process_manager.start(self._script_path)

    def _start_process_manager(self):
        # Start the process manager
        process_manager_task = ProcessManagerTask(
            interval=self._process_manager_interval,
            process_manager=self._process_manager,
        )
        self._process_manager_heartbeat = Heartbeat(
            "process_manager", process_manager_task, None
        )
        self._process_manager_heartbeat.start()

    def stop(self):
        """Stop all running Lilota components.

        This includes:
          - Stopping the scheduler (if running)
          - Stopping process monitoring
          - Gracefully terminating worker processes

        Worker processes are first asked to terminate gracefully. If a worker
        does not exit within ``stop_worker_timeout`` seconds, it is forcefully killed.
        """
        if not self._is_started:
            return

        if self._mode in (LilotaMode.SCHEDULER, LilotaMode.ALL):
            self._stop_scheduler()

        if self._mode in (LilotaMode.WORKERS, LilotaMode.ALL):
            self._stop_process_manager()
            self._stop_workers()

        self._is_started = False

    def _stop_scheduler(self):
        self._scheduler.stop()

    def _stop_workers(self):
        self._process_manager.stop_all(self._stop_worker_timeout)

    def _stop_process_manager(self):
        if self._process_manager_heartbeat:
            self._process_manager_heartbeat.stop_and_join(
                timeout=self._stop_worker_timeout
            )
            self._process_manager_heartbeat = None

    def schedule(self, name: str, input: Any = None) -> UUID:
        """Schedule a task for execution.

        Args:
          name (str): Name of the registered task.
          input (Any, optional): Input payload for the task. Defaults to None.

        Returns:
          UUID: Identifier of the scheduled task.

        Raises:
          RuntimeError: If lilota has never been started, or if it only runs
            workers (mode WORKERS).
        """
        if self._mode == LilotaMode.WORKERS:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "A task cannot be scheduled in WORKERS mode because there is no "
                "scheduler. Use the mode SCHEDULER or ALL"
            )

        id = self._scheduler.schedule(name, input)

        if self.has_failed():
            self._scheduler._logger.warning(
                f"The task '{name}' ({id}) was scheduled, but no worker can execute "
                "it: a fatal error has stopped all workers. Call start() to start "
                "them again"
            )

        return id

    def cleanup(self, older_than: timedelta) -> dict[str, int]:
        """Delete old rows from the tables of lilota.

        Nothing else deletes them: every task, every log entry and every node
        stays in the database until this method is called. Call it from time to
        time, for example once a day. It works in every mode, whether lilota is
        started or not.

        These rows are deleted if they are older than ``older_than``:
          - Tasks that are finished: completed, failed, expired or cancelled.
            The age is counted from the time the task ended or expired.
          - Log entries. The age is counted from the time the entry was written.
          - Nodes with the status dead. The age is counted from the time the
            node was last seen.

        A task that is waiting or being executed, a failed or expired task that
        still waits for its retry, and a node that is alive are never deleted.

        Args:
          older_than (timedelta): The age from which on a row is deleted.
            ``timedelta(days=30)`` deletes what is older than 30 days.

        Returns:
          dict[str, int]: The number of deleted rows, with the keys ``tasks``,
          ``log_entries`` and ``nodes``.

        Raises:
          ValueError: If ``older_than`` is negative.
        """
        if older_than < timedelta(0):
            raise ValueError("older_than must not be negative")

        cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - older_than

        return {
            "tasks": self._task_store.delete_finished_tasks(cutoff),
            "log_entries": self._log_store.delete_log_entries(cutoff),
            "nodes": self._node_store.delete_dead_nodes(cutoff),
        }

    def get_all_nodes(self) -> list[Node]:
        """Retrieve all registered nodes: schedulers and workers.

        Returns:
            list[Node]: A list containing all nodes currently stored in the
            node store.
        """
        return self._node_store.get_all_nodes()

    def get_task_by_id(self, id: UUID):
        """Retrieve a task by its unique identifier.

        Args:
          id (UUID): Unique task identifier.

        Returns:
          Any: Task object associated with the given ID.
        """
        return self._task_store.get_task_by_id(id)

def __init__(
    self,
    db_url: str = DEFAULT_DB_URL,
    *,
    mode: LilotaMode = LilotaMode.ALL,
    script_path: str = None,
    number_of_workers: int = 1,
    scheduler_heartbeat_interval: float = 5,
    scheduler_timeout_sec: int = 20,
    process_manager_interval: float = 1.0,
    stop_worker_timeout: int = 60,
    logging_level=logging.INFO,
    on_fatal_error: Callable[[str], None] = None,
):
    """Create a new Lilota runtime instance.

    Args:
      db_url (str):
        Database connection URL used by the scheduler.

      mode (LilotaMode, optional):
        Execution mode controlling whether the scheduler, workers,
        or both are started. Defaults to ALL.

      script_path (str):
        Path to a Python script that defines and registers Lilota tasks.
        Each worker process executes this script as its entry point.
        The script must call ``worker.start()``. If it ends without
        starting a worker, all workers are stopped and the failure is
        reported through ``error``.

      number_of_workers (int, optional):
        Number of worker processes to spawn. A worker executes one task
        at a time, so this is the number of tasks that can be executed
        in parallel. Defaults to 1 and cannot exceed the number of CPU
        cores * 5.

      scheduler_heartbeat_interval (float, optional):
        Interval in seconds between scheduler node heartbeats.
        Defaults to 5 seconds.

      scheduler_timeout_sec (int, optional):
        Time in seconds after which a node is considered inactive
        if no heartbeat is received. Defaults to 20 seconds.

      stop_worker_timeout (int, optional):
        Maximum time in seconds to wait for worker processes to
        exit gracefully before they are forcefully killed.
        Defaults to 60 seconds.

      logging_level (int, optional):
        Logging level used by the scheduler. Defaults to logging.INFO.

      on_fatal_error (Callable[[str], None], optional):
        Function that is called when a fatal error has stopped all
        workers. It gets the error, which is also what ``error``
        returns. It is called in the thread that monitors the workers,
        so it should return quickly, and it must not call ``stop()``.
    """
    if mode in (LilotaMode.WORKERS, LilotaMode.ALL):
        if number_of_workers <= 0:
            raise ValueError("number_of_workers must be > 0 in WORKER or ALL mode")

        number_of_cpus = cpu_count()
        max_workers = number_of_cpus * 5
        if number_of_workers > max_workers:
            raise ValueError(
                f"number_of_workers cannot be greater than {max_workers}"
            )

    self._db_url = db_url
    self._mode = mode
    self._script_path = script_path
    self._number_of_workers = number_of_workers
    self._process_manager_interval = process_manager_interval
    self._stop_worker_timeout = stop_worker_timeout
    self._process_manager_heartbeat: Heartbeat = None
    self._process_manager = ProcessManager(on_fatal_error=self._handle_fatal_error)
    self._on_fatal_error = on_fatal_error
    self._error = None
    self._error_event = threading.Event()
    atexit.register(self._process_manager.stop_all)

    if mode in (LilotaMode.SCHEDULER, LilotaMode.ALL):
        self._scheduler = LilotaScheduler(
            db_url=db_url,
            node_heartbeat_interval=scheduler_heartbeat_interval,
            node_timeout_sec=scheduler_timeout_sec,
            logging_level=logging_level,
        )

    self._node_store = NodeStore(self._db_url, None)
    self._task_store = TaskStore(self._db_url, None)
    self._log_store = LogStore(self._db_url)
    self._is_started = False

class ProcessManager:
    def __init__(self, on_fatal_error=None):
        """Initializes the ProcessManager.

        Args:
          on_fatal_error (Callable[[str], None] | None): Optional callback that is
            invoked when a managed process exits with an error. The callback
            receives the stderr output of the failed process.
        """
        self._on_fatal_error = on_fatal_error
        self._processes: List[ManagedProcess] = []

    def start(self, script_path: str, restarts: int = 0) -> subprocess.Popen:
        """Starts a new subprocess running the given Python script.

        The process is launched using the current Python interpreter and added
        to the internal list of managed processes.

        What the process writes to stdout goes to the stdout of the current
        process. What it writes to stderr is read by a ``WorkerErrorOutput``,
        which passes it on to the stderr of the current process.

        The process is told the ID of the current process, so that a worker
        stops itself when the current process is gone (see
        ``ParentProcessTask`` in ``lilota.worker``).

        Args:
          script_path (str): Path to the Python script to execute.
          restarts (int): How many times in a row the script has been restarted
            because its process had died. Only ``monitor`` passes it.

        Returns:
          subprocess.Popen: The Popen object representing the started process.
        """
        proc = subprocess.Popen(
            # -u: without it Python buffers the output of the worker whenever it does
            # not go to a terminal. The text would show up late, and never if the
            # worker is stopped before its buffer is full.
            [sys.executable, "-u", script_path],
            # stdout is not redirected. A pipe that nobody reads from blocks the
            # worker as soon as it is full.
            stdout=None,
            stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
            text=True,
            errors="replace",
            # Nothing in this process can stop the workers if it is killed. They have
            # to notice on their own that it is gone.
            env={**os.environ, WORKER_PARENT_PID_ENV: str(os.getpid())},
            # The worker gets its own session and process group, so that a signal to
            # the group reaches the worker and what its tasks have started, and
            # nothing else. Not with preexec_fn=os.setsid: that runs Python code in
            # the forked process, which can deadlock when this process has more
            # threads. No effect on Windows, where creationflags does it.
            start_new_session=True,
            creationflags=subprocess.CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP if os.name == "nt" else 0,
        )

        self._processes.append(ManagedProcess(proc, script_path, restarts))
        return proc

    def monitor(self):
        """Monitors managed processes for termination and handles restarts.

        Iterates over all managed processes and checks whether they have exited.

        A process that was killed is restarted using the original script path.
        That is a worker that stopped itself because its task has expired, or a
        process that was terminated by a signal. Such a worker has not failed by
        itself, so what it has written to stderr before does not matter.

        If a process ends on its own with a non-zero return code and has produced
        stderr output, the script has failed. All processes are stopped and the
        fatal error callback is invoked.

        The same happens if a process exits successfully. A started worker runs
        until it is stopped from the outside, so a script that ends on its own
        never started its worker.

        In all other cases the process is restarted as well.

        A worker that stopped itself because its task has expired is restarted at
        once. Every other process has died, and is restarted after a waiting
        time: ``WORKER_RESTART_DELAY`` seconds, and twice as long with every
        restart in a row. After ``WORKER_RESTART_ATTEMPTS`` restarts in a row the
        script keeps dying. All processes are stopped and the fatal error callback
        is invoked. A process that has been running for
        ``WORKER_RESTART_RESET_TIME`` seconds before it died does not count as a
        restart in a row.
        """
        for mp in list(self._processes):
            # The process has died before, and waits for its restart
            if mp.restart_at is not None:
                if time.monotonic() >= mp.restart_at:
                    self._restart(mp, mp.restarts + 1)
                continue

            proc = mp.proc
            returncode = proc.poll()

            if returncode is not None:  # process exited
                # This cannot be debugged. Use print statements because if the worker is killed also the debugger stops.
                stderr = mp.error_output.text()

                # = 0: Process exited successfully
                # > 0: Process exited with an error
                # < 0: Process was terminated by a signal (Unix only)
                was_killed = (
                    returncode < 0 or returncode == WORKER_EXIT_CODE_TASK_EXPIRED
                )

                # Error handling in case of an exception. Only for a process that
                # ended on its own: the stderr output of a worker is everything it
                # has written since it was started, so a killed worker that once
                # wrote a warning would be taken for a script that failed.
                if not was_killed and returncode != 0 and stderr:
                    self._handle_error(stderr)
                    return

                # A started worker never exits on its own. Restarting the script would
                # only end up in an endless loop.
                if returncode == 0:
                    self._handle_error(
                        f"The worker script '{mp.script_path}' exited without starting a worker. "
                        "Did you forget to call worker.start()?"
                    )
                    return

                # A worker that stopped itself because its task has expired has not
                # died. It is restarted at once, however often that happens.
                if returncode == WORKER_EXIT_CODE_TASK_EXPIRED:
                    self._restart(mp, 0)
                    continue

                # The process has died. If it has been running for a while, it is
                # not one that keeps dying.
                restarts = mp.restarts
                if time.monotonic() - mp.started_at >= WORKER_RESTART_RESET_TIME:
                    restarts = 0

                # Restarting it again and again would go on for as long as the
                # application runs, without anybody being told
                if restarts >= WORKER_RESTART_ATTEMPTS:
                    self._handle_error(
                        self._describe_death(mp, restarts, returncode, stderr)
                    )
                    return

                # Restart the process, after a waiting time that doubles with every
                # restart in a row
                mp.restarts = restarts
                mp.restart_at = time.monotonic() + WORKER_RESTART_DELAY * 2**restarts

    def _restart(self, mp: ManagedProcess, restarts: int):
        self._processes.remove(mp)
        self.start(mp.script_path, restarts)

    def _describe_death(
        self, mp: ManagedProcess, restarts: int, returncode: int, stderr: str
    ) -> str:
        if returncode < 0:
            try:
                signal_name = signal.Signals(-returncode).name
            except ValueError:
                signal_name = str(-returncode)
            end = f"was killed by the signal {signal_name}"
        else:
            end = f"ended with the exit code {returncode}"

        error = (
            f"The worker script '{mp.script_path}' was restarted {restarts} times in "
            f"a row, and its process died every time. The last time it {end}."
        )

        # What the process has written before it died may tell why
        if stderr:
            error += f"\n{stderr}"

        return error

    def _handle_error(self, stderr: str):
        # Stop all processes
        self.stop_all()

        # Signal to caller
        if self._on_fatal_error:
            self._on_fatal_error(stderr)

    def stop_all(self, timeout: float = 5.0):
        """Stops all managed processes gracefully, then forcefully if needed.

        Attempts to terminate all running processes. If a process does not exit
        within the specified timeout, it is forcefully killed. After stopping,
        the internal process list is cleared.

        Args:
          timeout (float): Maximum time in seconds to wait for each process to
            terminate gracefully before forcefully killing it. Defaults to 5.0.
        """
        for mp in self._processes:
            proc = mp.proc
            if proc.poll() is None:
                self._terminate(proc)

        for mp in self._processes:
            proc = mp.proc
            try:
                proc.wait(timeout=timeout)
            except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                self._kill(proc)

        # Let the readers finish, so that the pipes are closed
        for mp in self._processes:
            mp.error_output.join(WorkerErrorOutput.JOIN_TIMEOUT)

        self._processes.clear()

    def _terminate(self, proc):
        if os.name == "nt":
            proc.send_signal(signal.CTRL_BREAK_EVENT)
        else:
            os.killpg(os.getpgid(proc.pid), signal.SIGTERM)

    def _kill(self, proc):
        if os.name == "nt":
            proc.kill()
        else:
            os.killpg(os.getpgid(proc.pid), signal.SIGKILL)

def start(self, script_path: str, restarts: int = 0) -> subprocess.Popen:
    """Starts a new subprocess running the given Python script.

    The process is launched using the current Python interpreter and added
    to the internal list of managed processes.

    What the process writes to stdout goes to the stdout of the current
    process. What it writes to stderr is read by a ``WorkerErrorOutput``,
    which passes it on to the stderr of the current process.

    The process is told the ID of the current process, so that a worker
    stops itself when the current process is gone (see
    ``ParentProcessTask`` in ``lilota.worker``).

    Args:
      script_path (str): Path to the Python script to execute.
      restarts (int): How many times in a row the script has been restarted
        because its process had died. Only ``monitor`` passes it.

    Returns:
      subprocess.Popen: The Popen object representing the started process.
    """
    proc = subprocess.Popen(
        # -u: without it Python buffers the output of the worker whenever it does
        # not go to a terminal. The text would show up late, and never if the
        # worker is stopped before its buffer is full.
        [sys.executable, "-u", script_path],
        # stdout is not redirected. A pipe that nobody reads from blocks the
        # worker as soon as it is full.
        stdout=None,
        stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
        text=True,
        errors="replace",
        # Nothing in this process can stop the workers if it is killed. They have
        # to notice on their own that it is gone.
        env={**os.environ, WORKER_PARENT_PID_ENV: str(os.getpid())},
        # The worker gets its own session and process group, so that a signal to
        # the group reaches the worker and what its tasks have started, and
        # nothing else. Not with preexec_fn=os.setsid: that runs Python code in
        # the forked process, which can deadlock when this process has more
        # threads. No effect on Windows, where creationflags does it.
        start_new_session=True,
        creationflags=subprocess.CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP if os.name == "nt" else 0,
    )

    self._processes.append(ManagedProcess(proc, script_path, restarts))
    return proc

Reads what a worker process writes to stderr, for as long as the process runs.

The stderr of a worker process is connected to a pipe, because the text is needed when the process fails (see ProcessManager.monitor). A pipe only holds a limited amount of data. class WorkerErrorOutput(threading.Thread):
    """Reads what a worker process writes to stderr, for as long as the process runs.

    The stderr of a worker process is connected to a pipe, because the text is needed
    when the process fails (see ``ProcessManager.monitor``). A pipe only holds a
    limited amount of data. If nobody reads from it, the worker blocks as soon as it
    is full, in the middle of whatever task it is executing. This thread therefore
    reads every line the moment it is written.

    Each line is passed on to the stderr of the current process, so that warnings and
    tracebacks of a worker are visible where the output of the application is. The
    last lines are also kept, to be reported as the error if the process fails.
    """

    # How much of the output is kept for the error message. A worker can run for
    # weeks, so keeping everything is not an option.
    MAX_LINES = 200
    MAX_LINE_LENGTH = 8192

    # How long to wait for the rest of the output after the process has exited. The
    # pipe stays open for as long as a process started by the worker still uses it.
    JOIN_TIMEOUT = 2.0

    def __init__(self, proc: subprocess.Popen):
        """Initializes the reader. It starts reading when ``start()`` is called.

        Args:
          proc (subprocess.Popen): Worker process, started with ``stderr=PIPE``
            in text mode.
        """
        super().__init__(name=f"lilota_worker_stderr_{proc.pid}", daemon=True)
        self._stream = proc.stderr
        self._last_lines: deque[str] = deque(maxlen=self.MAX_LINES)
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def run(self) -> None:
        """Reads the stream until the worker process closes it."""
        try:
            # readline with a limit instead of iterating over the stream: a worker
            # that writes megabytes without a line break is read in pieces.
            while line := self._stream.readline(self.MAX_LINE_LENGTH):
                with self._lock:
                    self._last_lines.append(line)
                self._forward(line)
        except ValueError:
            # The stream was closed while reading from it
            pass
        finally:
            self._stream.close()

    def _forward(self, line: str) -> None:
        # Nothing that goes wrong here may stop the reading. sys.stderr is looked up
        # for every line, so that an application that replaces it gets the output.
        try:
            if sys.stderr is not None:
                sys.stderr.write(line)
                sys.stderr.flush()
        except Exception:
            pass

    def text(self) -> str:
        """Returns the last lines the worker process wrote to stderr.

        Meant to be called after the process has exited. Waits for the remaining
        output to be read, but not longer than ``JOIN_TIMEOUT`` seconds.

        Returns:
          str: At most the last ``MAX_LINES`` lines, or an empty string if the
          process wrote nothing to stderr.
        """
        self.join(self.JOIN_TIMEOUT)
        with self._lock:
            return "".join(self._last_lines)

class LilotaNode(ABC):
    """Abstract base class for all Lilota nodes.

    A node represents a running component in the Lilota system, such as a
    scheduler or a worker. This class handles common functionality including:

    - database initialization and migrations
    - node lifecycle management
    - node status updates
    - heartbeat management
    - access to node and task stores
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        *,
        db_url: str,
        node_type: NodeType,
        node_heartbeat_interval: float,
        node_timeout_sec: int,
        logger_name: str,
        logging_level,
    ):
        """Initialize a Lilota node.

        Args:
          db_url (str): Database connection URL.
          node_type (NodeType): Type of node (`scheduler` or `worker`).
          node_heartbeat_interval (float): Interval in seconds between node
            heartbeat updates.
          node_timeout_sec (int): Time in seconds after which a node is
            considered inactive if no heartbeat is received.
          logger_name (str): Name of the logger used by the node.
          logging_level (int): Logging level used for the node logger.
        """

        self._db_url = db_url
        self._node_type = node_type
        self._node_heartbeat_interval = node_heartbeat_interval
        self._node_heartbeat_join_timeout_in_sec = 60
        self._node_timeout_sec = node_timeout_sec
        self._node_id = None
        self._node_store = None
        self._task_store = None
        self._heartbeat: Heartbeat = None
        self._logging_level = logging_level
        self._is_started = False

        # Upgrade the database
        upgrade_db(self._db_url)

        # Setup logging
        self._logger = configure_logging(self._db_url, logger_name, logging_level)

    def start(self):
        """Start the node.

        Initializes the node in the database, sets its status to ``RUNNING``,
        and triggers the node-specific startup logic implemented in
        ``_on_started()``.

        Raises:
          Exception: If the node is already started.
        """

        # Check if the node is already started
        if self._is_started:
            raise Exception("The node is already started")

        if not self._node_id:
            # Create stores
            self._node_store = NodeStore(self._db_url, self._logger)
            self._task_store = TaskStore(self._db_url, self._logger)

            # Create node with status IDLE
            self._node_id = self._node_store.create_node(
                self._node_type, NodeStatus.RUNNING
            )

            # Create a context logger
            self._logger = create_context_logger(self._logger, node_id=self._node_id)
        else:
            # Change status to RUNNING
            self._node_store.update_node_status(self._node_id, NodeStatus.RUNNING)

        # Set the node as started
        self._is_started = True

        # On started
        self._on_started()

    def stop(self):
        """Stop the node.

        Updates the node status to ``STOPPING``, executes subclass-specific
        shutdown logic via ``_on_stop()``, and then sets the node status to
        ``IDLE``.

        Raises:
          Exception: If the node was not started.
        """

        # Check if the node was started
        if not self._is_started:
            raise Exception("The node cannot be stopped because it was not started")

        # Stop node heartbeat
        self._stop_node_heartbeat()

        # Change status to IDLE
        self._node_store.update_node_status(self._node_id, NodeStatus.IDLE)

        # Log Node stopped message
        self._logger.debug("Node stopped")

        # Set the node as not started
        self._is_started = False

    def get_nodes(self):
        """Return all nodes currently registered in the system.

        Returns:
          list: A list of node records.
        """
        return self._node_store.get_all_nodes()

    def get_node(self):
        """Return the current node record.

        Returns:
          Any | None: The node record if the node has been created,
          otherwise ``None``.
        """
        return self._node_store.get_node_by_id(self._node_id) if self._node_id else None

    def get_task_by_id(self, id: UUID):
        """Retrieve a task by its identifier.

        Args:
          id (UUID): Unique identifier of the task.

        Returns:
          Any: Task record associated with the given ID.
        """
        return self._task_store.get_task_by_id(id)

    def delete_task_by_id(self, id: UUID):
        """Delete a task from the system.

        Args:
          id (UUID): Unique identifier of the task.

        Returns:
          bool: True if the task was deleted, otherwise False.
        """
        self._logger.debug(f"Delete task with id {id}")
        success = self._task_store.delete_task_by_id(id)
        if success:
            self._logger.debug("Task deleted!")
        else:
            self._logger.debug("Task not deleted!")
        return success

    def _stop_node_heartbeat(self):
        # Stop heartbeat thread
        if self._heartbeat:
            self._heartbeat.stop_and_join(
                timeout=self._node_heartbeat_join_timeout_in_sec
            )
            self._heartbeat = None

    def _on_started(self):
        """Hook executed after the node has successfully started.

        Subclasses should implement this method to start any required
        background threads, heartbeats, or task loops.
        """
        pass

def start(self):
    """Start the node.

    Initializes the node in the database, sets its status to ``RUNNING``,
    and triggers the node-specific startup logic implemented in
    ``_on_started()``.

    Raises:
      Exception: If the node is already started.
    """

    # Check if the node is already started
    if self._is_started:
        raise Exception("The node is already started")

    if not self._node_id:
        # Create stores
        self._node_store = NodeStore(self._db_url, self._logger)
        self._task_store = TaskStore(self._db_url, self._logger)

        # Create node with status IDLE
        self._node_id = self._node_store.create_node(
            self._node_type, NodeStatus.RUNNING
        )

        # Create a context logger
        self._logger = create_context_logger(self._logger, node_id=self._node_id)
    else:
        # Change status to RUNNING
        self._node_store.update_node_status(self._node_id, NodeStatus.RUNNING)

    # Set the node as started
    self._is_started = True

    # On started
    self._on_started()

def stop(self):

    Updates the node status to ``STOPPING``, executes subclass-specific
    shutdown logic via ``_on_stop()``, and then sets the node status to
    ``IDLE``.

    Raises:
      Exception: If the node was not started.
    """

    # Check if the node was started
    if not self._is_started:
        raise Exception("The node cannot be stopped because it was not started")

    # Set the node as not started
    self._is_started = False

class NodeHeartbeatTask(HeartbeatTask):
    """Heartbeat task used by Lilota nodes.

    This task periodically updates the ``last_seen_at`` timestamp of the
    associated node in the database to indicate that the node is still alive.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        interval: float,
        jitter: float,

        node_store: NodeStore,
        logger: logging.Logger,

        """Initialize the heartbeat task.

          interval (float): Interval in seconds between heartbeat executions.

          node_id (UUID): Unique identifier of the node.
          node_store (NodeStore): Store used for node operations.

        """
        super().__init__(interval, jitter)
        self._node_id = node_id
        self._node_store = node_store
        self._logger = logger

    def execute(self):
        """Execute the heartbeat update.

        Updates the ``last_seen_at`` field of the node in the database.
        Any errors are logged without interrupting the heartbeat loop.

            self._node_store.update_node_last_seen_at(self._node_id)

            self._logger.exception(
                f"Heartbeat update failed for node_id '{self._node_id}'"

class LilotaScheduler(LilotaNode):
    """Scheduler node responsible for creating and managing tasks.

    The scheduler registers itself as a scheduler node in the system and
    periodically sends heartbeats to indicate it is alive. Its main role
    is to create tasks and store them in the task store for workers to
    execute.
    """

    LOGGER_NAME = "lilota.scheduler"

    def __init__(
        self,
        db_url: str,
        node_heartbeat_interval: float = 5.0,
        node_timeout_sec: int = 20,
        logging_level=logging.INFO,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        """Initialize the scheduler node.

        Args:
          db_url (str): Database connection URL.
          node_heartbeat_interval (float, optional): Interval in seconds between
            node heartbeats. Defaults to 5.0.
          node_timeout_sec (int, optional): Time in seconds before a node is
            considered inactive. Defaults to 20.
          logging_level (int, optional): Logging level used by the scheduler.
            Defaults to logging.INFO.
          **kwargs: Additional keyword arguments passed to the parent
            ``LilotaNode`` initializer.
        """
        super().__init__(
            db_url=db_url,
            node_type=NodeType.SCHEDULER,
            node_heartbeat_interval=node_heartbeat_interval,
            node_timeout_sec=node_timeout_sec,
            logger_name=self.LOGGER_NAME,
            logging_level=logging_level,
            **kwargs,
        )

    def _on_started(self):
        # Start heartbeat thread
        heartbeat_task = NodeHeartbeatTask(
            self._node_heartbeat_interval,
            None,
            self._node_id,
            self._node_store,
            self._logger,
        )
        self._heartbeat = Heartbeat(
            f"scheduler_heartbeat_{self._node_id}", heartbeat_task, self._logger
        )
        self._heartbeat.start()

        # Log Node started message
        self._logger.debug("Node started")

    def _on_stop(self):
        # Stop heartbeat thread
        self._stop_node_heartbeat()

    def schedule(self, name: str, input: Any = None) -> UUID:
        """Create and store a new task.

        Args:
          name (str): Name of the registered task.
          input (Any, optional): Input payload for the task. Defaults to None.

        Returns:
          UUID: Identifier of the created task.

        Raises:
          RuntimeError: If the scheduler has never been started.
        """
        # The stores are created when the node is started for the first time
        if self._task_store is None:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "A task cannot be scheduled because the scheduler was not started. "
                "Call start() first"
            )

        self._logger.debug(f"Create task (name: '{name}', input: {input})")
        return self._task_store.create_task(name, input)

    def has_unfinished_tasks(self):
        """Check whether there are unfinished tasks in the system.

        Returns:
          bool: True if unfinished tasks exist, otherwise False.
        """
        return self._task_store.has_unfinished_tasks()
