def to_json(data: Any) -> Any:
    """Convert the return value of a task function to data that can be stored as JSON.

    - `None`, `bool`, `int`, `float` and `str` stay as they are.
    - A `dict`, a `list` and a `tuple` are converted value by value. A tuple
      becomes a list.
    - A `ModelProtocol` object and a dataclass become a dictionary.
    - A `datetime`, a `date` and a `time` become text in ISO 8601 format.
    - A `UUID` and a `Decimal` become text.

    Args:
        data (Any): The return value to convert.

    Returns:
        Any: Data that only consists of JSON values.

    Raises:
        TypeError: If `data` is or contains a value of any other type.
    """
    if data is None or isinstance(data, (bool, int, float, str)):
        return data

    if isinstance(data, dict):
        return {key: to_json(value) for key, value in data.items()}

    if isinstance(data, (list, tuple)):
        return [to_json(value) for value in data]

    # ModelProtocol
    if isinstance(data, ModelProtocol):
        return to_json(data.as_dict())

    # Dataclass. The class itself is not a value.
    if is_dataclass(data) and not isinstance(data, type):
        return to_json(asdict(data))

    if isinstance(data, (datetime, date, time)):
        return data.isoformat()

    if isinstance(data, (UUID, Decimal)):
        return str(data)

    raise TypeError(
        f"Unsupported type: {type(data).__name__}. Expected a JSON value, a "
        "ModelProtocol, a dataclass, a datetime, a date, a time, a UUID or a Decimal."
    )

docs.title: Retry mechanism
docs.text:
The Retry mechanism is responsible for identifying failed or expired tasks and scheduling retries in a safe, concurrent environment. It ensures that:

  • Tasks are retried only if eligible
  • Duplicate retries are prevented
  • Concurrency conflicts are handled via optimistic locking
  • Retry attempts are limited and delayed progressively

In lilota, you have to specify the max attempts for each task. By default it is set to 1.

The max attempts can be set when registering a task.

worker = LilotaWorker(
  ...
)

@worker.task(max_attempts=5)

docs.title: What max_attempts means
docs.text:
max_attempts is how often a task is executed at most. The first execution counts.

max_attempts A task that fails every time 1 (default) is executed once and is not retried. 3 is executed three times: once, followed by two retries.

docs.title: When a task is retried
docs.text:
A task is retried if it has attempts left and

  • its function raised an exception (status failed), or
  • it ran longer than its timeout (status expired, see Task timeout).

A task function that raises an exception does not stop the worker. The worker stores the exception in the error column of the task, sets its status to failed and goes on with the next task.

One kind of failed task is never retried: a task whose function has returned, but whose return value could not be stored. See Task registration.

docs.title: How a task is retried
docs.text:
A retry is a new task: a new row in lilota_task with the same name and the same input.

  • Its attempts column counts one further. The task you scheduled is attempt 1, its first retry is attempt 2.
  • Its previous_task_id column is the ID of the task it retries.
  • The task that failed keeps its status and its error, and its retried_at column says when the retry was created.

The ID returned by schedule therefore always is the ID of the first attempt.

A retry does not start at once. It waits 5 seconds for every attempt that has been made: 5 seconds before the second attempt, 10 seconds before the third.

Retries are created by the worker that currently is the leader, with its heartbeat (see Worker maintenance). This adds a few seconds. It takes longer if the worker that was stopped was the leader itself, because another worker has to become the leader first.

docs.title: Upgrading from lilota 1.2.0 or older
docs.text:
Two things were different up to 1.2.0:

  • A task function that raised an exception stopped all workers. The task was never retried, and tasks scheduled afterwards were not executed.
  • A task was executed once more than max_attempts said. With the default of 1, a task that ran into its timeout was executed twice.

Nothing has to be changed in your application. If you relied on the additional execution, raise max_attempts of the task by one.

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text:
lilota.stop()

In a web application, you will usually not need to call this explicitly. You start lilota once, then schedule tasks as needed.

As long as your application is running, lilota can continue running and waiting for tasks to be scheduled.

If you do call stop, lilota will stop the started scheduler and all running workers.

docs.title: The application ends without stopping lilota
docs.text:
An application does not always get the chance to stop its workers:

  • it is killed, for example with kill -9
  • it crashes
  • the operating system ends it because it used too much memory
  • it is terminated and does not handle the signal

Workers do not keep running in that case. Once a second each worker checks whether the process that started it is still there. If it is gone, the worker stops itself. Processes that a task has started are stopped with it.

Before it stops, the worker writes a warning to the lilota_log table:

The worker stops because the process that started it is gone

A task that the worker is executing at that moment is not finished. It is handled like the task of a worker that was killed. See Error handling.

A worker script that you start yourself, without the Lilota class, is not affected. It keeps running when the process that started it has ended.

Note: This works on Linux and macOS. On Windows a worker does not notice that the application is gone and keeps running.

docs.title: Upgrading from lilota 1.2.1 or older
docs.text:
Up to 1.2.1 workers kept running when the application had ended without stopping them. They took tasks and executed them with the code they were started with, and every start of the application added more workers.

Nothing has to be changed in your application. Workers that an older version has left behind do not stop on their own. Look for them once after the upgrade and end them, for example with ps ax | grep myscript.py.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Before a function can be executed by LilotaWorker, it must be registered as a task. A task is simply a Python function that is registered using the @worker.task decorator. Once registered, the task can be scheduled using:

lilota.schedule("task-name")

docs.title: Basic task
docs.text:
The simplest task does not require input or output.

myscript.py

from lilota.worker import LilotaWorker

worker = LilotaWorker()

@worker.task
def hello_world():
  print("Hello World")

By default a task is regsitered using the method name (here "hello_world"). Before a lilota instance needs to be created and started:

lilota = Lilota(
  script_path="sample/myscript.py"
)
lilota.start()

After that the task can be scheduled:

task_id = lilota.schedule("hello-world")

A task name can also be specified if needed.

@worker.task("mytask")
def hello_world():
  print("Hello World")

When scheduling the task this name is used.

task_id = lilota.schedule("mytask")

docs.title: Tasks with input and output models
docs.text:
Tasks can optionally define one input model and one output model. The input model describes the data that the task expects. The output model describes the structure of the result produced by the task.

Using models provides several advantages:

  • clearer task interfaces
  • type safety
  • structured task inputs and outputs
  • easier serialization

Currently, lilota supports dataclasses, dictionaries, and objects implementing ModelProtocol.

docs.title: Define input and output models
docs.text:
• Input and output models are optional
  • You do not have to use dataclasses for these models. You can use any serializable model, such as pydantic models.
  • It is only important that the models are serializable, since they are stored in the database.
  • lilota uses a ModelProtocol. To comply with it, you only need to define an as_dict method. A full example using pydantic can be found here: 3-add-two-numbers-using-pydantic
  • lilota also supports passing a TaskContext instance to the task function. It contains a progress field (of type TaskProgress) that can be used to update progress information in the database. It also contains a logger field (of type logging.Logger) that can be used to use the logging mechanism of Lilota. A full example using the progress field can be found here: 5-setting-task-progress-manually

docs.title: Full example with input and output model
docs.text:
The following example defines a task that adds two numbers.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from lilota.worker import LilotaWorker
from lilota.models import Task


@dataclass
class AddInput:
  a: int
  b: int


@dataclass
class AddOutput:
  sum: int


worker = LilotaWorker()


@worker.task
def add(data: AddInput) -> AddOutput:
  return AddOutput(sum=data.a + data.b)


def main():
  worker.start()


if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When the task is scheduled:

lilota.schedule("add", AddInput(a=2, b=3))

the input model is automatically serialized before being stored in the database. When the task runs, lilota automatically deserializes the data back into the input model:

def add(data: AddInput) -> AddOutput

The returned output model is then serialized again before being stored as the task result.

docs.title: Accessing the Result
docs.text:
Task results are stored as a dictionary in the database. To reconstruct the output model, you can create the object manually:

add_output = AddOutput(**task.output)

docs.title: What a task can return
docs.text:
The return value of a task function is stored as JSON in the output column of the task. A task function can return

  • a dataclass, a dictionary or an object implementing ModelProtocol
  • any other JSON value: a string, a number, a boolean, a list or None
@worker.task
def count_words(data: dict[str, str]) -> int:
  return len(data["text"].split())

Values that JSON does not know are converted, also inside of a dataclass, a dictionary or a list:

Returned value Stored as datetime, date, time text in ISO 8601 format, like 2026-01-02T03:04:05+00:00 UUID text Decimal text, like 9.99, so that no digit is lost tuple list

docs.title: A return value that cannot be stored
docs.text:
A value of any other type cannot be stored, for example an object of a class of your own that has no as_dict method.

The task function has done its work at that point. Executing it again would do that work a second time. The task therefore

  • gets the status failed
  • is not retried, whatever max_attempts says. Its max_attempts column is set to the attempts it has made
  • gets an error that says so:
The task function succeeded, but its result could not be stored: Unsupported type: Report. Expected a JSON value, a ModelProtocol, a dataclass, a datetime, a date, a time, a UUID or a Decimal.

docs.title: Upgrading from lilota 1.2.1 or older
docs.text:
Up to 1.2.1 a task function could only return a dataclass, a dictionary or an object implementing ModelProtocol, and only with values that JSON knows. With any other return value the task was marked as failed after its function had returned, and it was executed again if it had attempts left.

Nothing has to be changed in your application. Tasks that failed for this reason are completed now.

docs.title: Tasks with setting progress manually
docs.text:
Some tasks run for a longer time and should report progress. LilotaWorker provides the TaskProgress helper for this purpose. It is part of the TaskContext object.

@worker.task
def do_something(task_context: TaskContext) -> None:
  for i in range(1, 101):
    task_context.progress.set(i)

worker = LilotaWorker()

docs.title: Tasks that use the lilota logger
docs.text:
It is possible to use the internal logging system from lilota. Via the TaskContext it can be injected to the task.

@worker.task
def only_logger(task_context: TaskContext) -> None:
  task_context.logger.info("Message from only_logger task")

docs.title: Task timeout
docs.text:
In a software application, it can happen that scheduled tasks are executed but never finish. This can occur for several reasons:

  • The task contains an infinite loop
  • The task simply takes too long to execute
  • The task is waiting indefinitely for an external service (e.g., API call, database, or network request)
  • A deadlock occurs (e.g., waiting on a locked resource)
  • Resource exhaustion (e.g., CPU, memory) prevents the task from progressing

To handle such situations, lilota provides a mechanism to deal with tasks that never complete by stopping the corresponding worker process. When this happens, the task is terminated and its status is set to expired.

In lilota, it is recommended to specify a timeout for each task.

The timeout can be set when registering a task.

worker = LilotaWorker(
  ...
)

@worker.task("my_task", timeout=timedelta(minutes=5))

The default timeout is 5 minutes. This can be adjusted using Python’s timedelta object. If None is specified, the timeout is disabled.

The worker process that was stopped is replaced by a new one, so the tasks that are waiting are still executed. The expired task is retried if it has attempts left. See Retry mechanism.

docs.title: A task that ends at the moment it expires
docs.text:
A task that ends just when its timeout is over is either completed or expired, never both. If the task was set to expired first, its result is not stored, and the task is retried if it has attempts left. The worker writes a warning to the lilota_log table:

The result of the task was not stored, because the task had ended before: it has run into its timeout, or it was deleted (id: 0d3c...)

The timeout is checked by another worker than the one that executes the task. If your workers run on several machines, their clocks have to be in sync. See Clocks on several machines.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: In a distributed environment, worker nodes must regularly perform maintenance tasks to ensure the system remains healthy and consistent. In lilota, this responsibility is handled automatically through the worker heartbeat mechanism and a lightweight leader election process.

docs.title: How Maintenance Works
docs.text:
Each worker periodically sends a heartbeat to indicate that it is alive. During this process, workers also participate in a leader election. At any given time, exactly one worker acts as the leader.

Only the elected leader performs maintenance tasks. This avoids duplicate work and ensures consistent system state across all workers.

docs.title: Maintenance Tasks
docs.text: When a worker becomes the leader, it executes the following maintenance tasks:

docs.title: 1. Cleanup of Dead Nodes
docs.text:
Workers that have not sent a heartbeat within a configured timeout are considered dead.

  • A cutoff timestamp is calculated based on the configured node timeout
  • All nodes with a last_seen_at older than this cutoff are marked as dead
  • The current worker (leader) is excluded from this process

This ensures that inactive or crashed workers do not remain in an inconsistent state.

The leader only looks for dead nodes when its own heartbeats have reached the database without a gap for as long as the node timeout. If the database could not be reached, or the whole machine stood still, the heartbeats of all workers are missing, and a worker that is alive must not be taken for dead. A worker that has just started therefore finds dead nodes after the node timeout at the earliest.

docs.title: 2. Tasks of Dead Nodes
docs.text:
A worker that dies cannot finish the tasks it has taken, and no other worker takes a task that belongs to another worker. The leader therefore gives these tasks back.

  • The task store looks for tasks that were taken or are being executed by a worker that is dead
  • These tasks get the status created again, as if no worker had taken them
  • The next worker that is free executes them

This is not counted as an attempt. The task is also executed again with the default max_attempts of 1.

A worker counts as dead when it has not sent a heartbeat within the node timeout, which is 20 seconds by default (node_timeout_sec). A task of a dead worker is therefore executed again after about that time.

The leader writes a warning to the lilota_log table:

Gave back 1 task(s) of dead node(s). They are executed again

Note: A task that is given back was ended in the middle and is executed again from the beginning. What it has done before, it does twice. The same happens if a worker is taken for dead although it is only not reachable for longer than the node timeout: its task is then executed by a second worker as well.

A task that has run into its timeout is not given back. It is handled as described in the next two sections.

docs.title: 3. Expiration of Overdue Tasks
docs.text:
Tasks that exceed their configured timeout are automatically marked as expired.

  • The task store checks for running tasks whose expiration time has passed
  • These tasks are updated to the expired state

This prevents tasks from running indefinitely and ensures system stability.

More information can be found here.

docs.title: 4. Retry of Tasks
docs.text:
Tasks that have failed or expired are retried if they have attempts left.

  • The task store looks for failed and expired tasks that were not retried yet
  • For each of them a new task is created that is executed after a delay

More information can be found here.

docs.title: Fault Tolerance
docs.text:
Maintenance execution is designed to be safe and resilient:

  • If maintenance fails, the error is logged but does not stop the worker
  • The heartbeat process continues running regardless of failures
  • Leadership is automatically renewed or reassigned if a leader becomes unavailable

docs.title: Worker output
docs.text:
Every worker is a Python process of its own, started by lilota. What a task function writes with print, or what a library it uses writes as a warning, comes from that process and not from your application.

lilota shows this output where the output of your application is shown.

docs.title: Output on stdout
docs.text:
What a worker writes to stdout goes to the stdout of your application: to the terminal you started the application in, or to the log of its container.

@worker.task
def hello_world():
  print("Hello World")

Hello World appears as soon as the task has printed it. Workers are started with python -u, so the text does not wait in a buffer when the output of your application is written to a file or a pipe instead of a terminal.

docs.title: Output on stderr
docs.text:
What a worker writes to stderr, such as warnings or the traceback of an exception, is passed on line by line to the stderr of your application. It is written to sys.stderr, so an application that replaces sys.stderr receives it there.

Writing to stderr is not an error. A worker that writes a warning keeps running.

lilota also keeps the last 200 lines a worker has written to stderr. If the worker process fails, these lines are the fatal error reported by the error property of the Lilota class. See Error handling.

docs.title: Upgrading from lilota 1.2.0 or older
docs.text:
Up to 1.2.0 the output of a worker was collected but never read while the worker was running. It was not shown anywhere, and a worker that had written about 64 KB stopped in the middle of its task, because there was no room left for more output.

Nothing has to be changed in your application. Be aware that output of your tasks that was invisible before is shown now.
